items.followUp: State the octet and duplet rules and give one example of an atom that follows each rule.

rubric.why: The octet rule describes the stable outer-shell arrangement of eight electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atoms tend to attain eight electrons in their outermost shell.

rubric.why: The duplet rule describes a stable arrangement of two electrons in the first shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atoms tend to attain two electrons in their first shell.

modelAnswer: Octet rule: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to attain eight electrons in their outermost shell.
Duplet rule: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to attain two electrons in their first shell.

items.followUp: Define a single covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond consists of two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms.

rubric.why: An example must identify a molecule or bond containing a double covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example such as O₂ (O=O) or CO₂ (C=O).

modelAnswer: A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
Example: In an oxygen molecule, O=O, the two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding is an attraction involving hydrogen and an electronegative atom.
rubric.description: Identifies hydrogen bonding as an attractive force involving hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as an attraction or intermolecular force involving hydrogen and an electronegative atom.

rubric.why: The common atoms involved in hydrogen bonding are fluorine, oxygen and nitrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming or symbolically identifying F, O and N.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attractive force involving a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom.
It commonly occurs when hydrogen is bonded to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen and is attracted to one of these atoms in a neighbouring molecule.

items.followUp: What is the value of absolute zero on the Celsius and Kelvin scales?

rubric.why: Absolute zero is the zero point on the Kelvin scale.

rubric.description: Gives the Celsius value or meaning.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating approximately −273 °C, or that it is the lowest possible temperature at which molecular motion ceases.

modelAnswer: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, at which molecular motion theoretically ceases.

items.followUp: How does increasing temperature affect the rate of evaporation?

rubric.why: Stronger intermolecular forces make it harder for molecules to escape from the liquid.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of stronger forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that stronger intermolecular forces slow evaporation.

rubric.why: With weaker intermolecular forces, molecules escape more readily and evaporation is faster.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of weaker forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that weaker intermolecular forces increase the rate of evaporation.

modelAnswer: Strong intermolecular forces hold liquid molecules together, so fewer molecules escape and evaporation is slower.
Weak intermolecular forces allow molecules to escape more easily, so evaporation is faster.

items.followUp: Define a non-aqueous solution and give one example.

rubric.why: An aqueous solution has water as its solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water is the solvent.

rubric.why: A correct example must be a solute dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as salt dissolved in water.

modelAnswer: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
Example: Salt dissolved in water forms an aqueous solution.

items.followUp: A solution contains 8 g of solute in 200 mL of solution. Calculate its percentage mass/volume concentration.

rubric.why: The formula compares the solute mass in grams with the solution volume in millilitres.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula: % m/v = (mass of solute in g ÷ volume of solution in mL) × 100.

rubric.why: The percentage expresses grams of solute per 100 mL of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that % m/v is the grams of solute present in 100 mL of solution.

modelAnswer: Percentage mass/volume is the mass of solute, in grams, present in 100 mL of solution.
% m/v = (mass of solute in g ÷ volume of solution in mL) × 100

items.followUp: Define a dilute solution and a concentrated solution.

rubric.why: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a specified temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains the maximum amount of dissolved solute at a given temperature.

rubric.why: An unsaturated solution can dissolve additional solute at that temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it can dissolve more solute at a given temperature.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature.
An unsaturated solution contains less than this amount and can dissolve more solute at that temperature.
